## From cand_0003 (same capability, near-saturated split: 39/40 passing)
**6. The breadth mandate should scale with reachable score, because near saturation it inverts
the gate.** INSTRUCTIONS says breadth "is the goal", that a one- or two-edit iteration is
"under-used", and to "ship a fix for each cluster". At 39/40 there is exactly ONE failing task:
reachable gain +0.025, while a single regression drives Δ to 0.000 and auto-rejects. So edits
#2..N have zero upside and unbounded downside — the brief is asking, in score terms, for
negative-EV work, and an optimizer that complies will reliably destroy a champion. Suggest the
brief compute reachable headroom (`#failing / n`) and switch register when it is below ~3 tasks:
"ship only edits whose target is a measured failure; adding unverifiable edits now costs more
than it can win." The current wording made me write a defence of narrowness in PROCESS.md
instead of just doing the right thing.
**7. The gate's resolvable effect size can exceed the entire remaining headroom, which makes a
correct fix statistically invisible.** Here 2·SE ≈ 0.096 (~4 tasks) but only 1 task (0.025) is
left to win. Per LEDGER's own rule a move under 2·SE lands in `unresolved` and "is NOT evidence
the edit did anything" — so a genuinely correct single-task fix gets stamped as resolving
nothing, and the next iteration is told not to reason about it. That is a trap: the run can
no longer distinguish "worked" from "did nothing". Suggest the framework detect
`headroom < 2·SE` and either raise trials on the remaining failures to shrink SE, or state
explicitly in the brief that the split is saturated and the objective has shifted to
held-out generalization / no-regression rather than val Δ.
**8. Point the proposer at the rejected candidate's ROLLOUTS, not just its diff.** RUNMAP
supplies each prior iteration's `PROCESS.md` + `diff.patch`, which tell you *what* was tried and
*which* tasks broke — but not *how*. The decisive artifact for me was
`.capevolve/run_suite/rollouts/val/<task>__<cand>__t0.json` for the tasks cand_0002 broke: that
is where I found the agent writing `round(v, 4)  # matches examples` and losing 1261 of 1280
cells. That single trace converted "avoid that area" into a transferable mechanism and is why I
dropped an edit I had already verified as effective. Copying the broken tasks' rollouts into
`./prior_iterations/<id>/broke/` would make this the default rather than something I only found
because I went looking in the live run dir.
**9. `compare_workbooks`' signature is an easy silent footgun for verification work.** It is
`compare_workbooks(gt_file, proc_file, instruction_type, answer_position)` — the last two are
easy to transpose, and doing so raises `ValueError: Cell-Level Manipulation is not a valid
coordinate or range` rather than anything suggesting argument order. Since the brief actively
asks proposers to verify contract edits against what the scorer compares, a one-line usage
example in the guidance (or a keyword-only signature) would save everyone that detour.
**10. Repeat of #2, now load-bearing twice: ship the passing-set fingerprint.** cand_0001 asked
for `PASSING_FINGERPRINTS.md`; this iteration needed exactly the same thing again and rebuilt it
by hand (which passing tasks have pre-filled cells *inside* `answer_position`, which have
gold-blank cells in the graded block, which legitimately use two-bound date logic). Both of my
draft's near-regressions were caught by that information. It is mechanically derivable from the
gold files the framework already has, and every iteration of every prose capability needs it.

## "Still open at a date" is a single-instant test (mechanism — measured against the real gold)
- What worked (shipped in cand_0003, RESULT pending): for a count of rows open at a named
instant `T`, **both** bounds use that same `T` — `start <= T and (end is None or end > T)`.
43436's gold formula is `COUNTIFS(..., C<="&EOMONTH(...), D>"&EOMONTH(...))`: EOMONTH on both
sides. Verified through the official `compare_workbooks`: mixed-instant → False,
single-instant → True (15/15). Robust to strictness — `end > T` and `end >= T` both pass.
- What didn't: the mixed form `start <= period_end and (end is None or end >= period_start)`.
It answers a *different* question ("open at any point during the period"), so it also counts
rows already closed earlier inside the period. Counts come out uniformly **too HIGH** — a
useful signature, since the scorer reports direction ("N cell(s) hold a number HIGHER").
- **Calibration cannot fix this class, and that is measured.** 43436's only sibling outside
`answer_position` is "Open as of today" = [1,2,1,0,1], and **both readings reproduce it**. So
a corroborate-against-a-sibling rule actively confirms the wrong reading. Ambiguity of
*definition* has to be closed by stating the definition; no amount of self-checking finds it.
## A prompt rule's HEADLINE is the recall unit — the gate must live in it (process mechanism)
- What didn't: putting a conditional rule's gate in the sentence *after* an unconditional
slogan. My first draft led with "Open/active at a point in time is a SINGLE-instant test —
put the same instant on both sides", gating it only in the next sentence. Measured danger:
59595 is correct *because* it uses two instants (`d-7 <= x <= d`); collapsing it breaks **15
of 16 cells**. 59595 is one of the four tasks cand_0002 broke — same failure shape.
- What worked: fold the gating condition into the bold headline, and add an explicit negative
carve-out naming the neighbouring shapes that must NOT change (rolling window, custom 24-h
bucket, date-range sum). Audited scope after: fires on the failing task only, zero passers.
## Verification-style prose is dangerous on this benchmark (confirmed by cand_0002's RESULT)
- What didn't (RESULT-confirmed, cand_0002 rejected, `broke={402-43, 560-12, 59595, 9569}`):
step-7 additions that tell the agent to corroborate its interpretation. Mechanism recovered
from cand_0002's own rollouts: 9569's agent wrote `earliest = round(v, 4)  # matches examples`
and turned **1261 of 1280 correct cells wrong**, while its verify round reported "Mismatch
count: 0" — **a self-recomputation check is circular: it cannot detect the error, but it does
license changing values.** 59595 got `if r <= 6: computed[r] = "n/a"`, 3 correct ints → str.
- Why it keeps backfiring: these workbooks put the worked example in the FIRST row of the answer
column, so "the most extreme / most checkable cell" is usually the **pre-filled stale cell
F14), and on 50768/53647/37456 the extreme cell's gold is **blank**. Any instruction aiming
the agent at that cell competes with the (correct) rule that a pre-fill is only a weak hint.
- Rule of thumb earned here: prefer stating a **domain definition** the reader cannot derive
over adding **interpretive procedure**. The first is bounded; the second changes behaviour on
every task that merely resembles the target.
## The val split is saturated — Δ is no longer an informative signal
- At 39/40, one task is the entire dynamic range (+0.025) while the gate's resolvable effect
size is 2·SE ≈ 0.096 (~4 tasks). **A true single-task fix is smaller than the measurement can
resolve**, and it is recorded as `unresolved`, not as a win. Meanwhile any regression is
immediately fatal (Δ → 0.000 auto-rejects). Consequence for whoever is next: extra edits have
zero expected upside and unbounded downside. Breadth was right at 12/40; at 39/40 the
score-maximising move is one verified edit and nothing else.

## Iteration cand_0003
- **Strategy tried: deliberately NARROW — one verified edit, against the instructions' explicit
push for breadth.** LEDGER row 1 (cand_0001, ACCEPT +0.675, breadth-first, 9 edits) and row 2
(cand_0002, REJECT −0.100, 4 tasks broken) together say the optimal edit count is a function
of **how much score is still reachable**, not a constant. At 12/40 breadth dominated. At
39/40 the entire reachable gain is 1 task = +0.025 while one regression is instantly fatal
(Δ → 0.000 auto-rejects), so edit #2 onward has **zero upside and unbounded downside**. I
ship one edit. If the framework wants breadth at 39/40 it is asking for negative-EV work;
the honest response is to say so in PROCESS.md rather than manufacture edits.
- **The adversarial-subagent pass earned its keep for the second run in a row — and this time it
caught MY edit, twice.** cand_0001's META_INSIGHTS said to always budget for it. I did, and
both verdicts were RISKY and both were right: (1) my first draft led with an *unconditional*
slogan and gated it only in the next sentence — 59595 is correct precisely because it uses two
different instants, and collapsing it breaks 15/16 cells (I re-derived that myself); (2) it
killed my second edit outright by finding, in cand_0002's own rollouts, the exact mechanism by
which that edit's ancestor broke 9569 (`round(v,4)` → 1261/1280 cells wrong, verify round
still reporting "Mismatch count: 0"). **Generalised lesson: the pass must review MY DRAFT, not
just the parent prose.** Reviewing the parent finds nothing; reviewing the draft found both.
- **New process rule: mine the REJECTED candidate's rollouts, not just its diff.** `LEDGER`
tells you *which* tasks a rejected edit broke; `.capevolve/run_suite/rollouts/val/<task>__<cand>__t0.json`
tells you *how*. Reading cand_0002's 9569 and 59595 rollouts turned "avoid that area" into a
named, transferable mechanism (self-recomputation checks are circular; the "most checkable
cell" is usually the pre-filled stale one). That is the single highest-information artifact in
the run and neither RUNMAP nor the instructions point at it.
- **Measure, don't reason — extended to the gate itself.** Two arithmetic checks reframed the
whole iteration: (a) 1/40 = 0.025 > 0.2·SE = 0.0096, so one fix *does* clear the bar; (b)
2·SE ≈ 0.096 ≈ 4 tasks, so a true one-task fix is **smaller than the measurement can
resolve** and will likely be stamped `unresolved` rather than `fixed`. Worth doing anyway
(it is the only reachable gain), but I expect the RESULT to look statistically flat even if
the edit works. Whoever reads that RESULT should not conclude the edit did nothing.
- **What I'd do differently:** I drafted edit 2 before checking it against the rejected
candidate's *mechanism*, and wasted effort verifying it was effective (it was) before
discovering it was unsafe (it was not). Order should be: check the rejected batch's mechanism
→ gate the draft → only then verify efficacy. Same lesson cand_0001 recorded (constraints
before drafting), re-learned in a new place.
- **Plateau signal: val is saturated and no longer an informative search signal.** 0.300 →
0.975 → (0.875, reverted). Remaining val headroom is one task of single-task domain
semantics. The lever to switch to for iterations 4-5 is **not** more val-directed prose but
generalization auditing: hunt for rules in the accepted prose that are over-broad on classes
absent from val but plausibly present in the held-out test (my own first draft was exactly
that bug). Prune or gate with measurement; adding has negative EV from here.
- **Budget note:** 2 iterations remain after this one. If cand_0003 is accepted, I would spend
at most one of them on the generalization audit above and explicitly bank the last rather than
spend it on a speculative edit against a saturated split — a rejected candidate costs the run
nothing but also teaches nothing when the split cannot resolve the effect.

# Matching the expected value exactly
The comparison is not fuzzy; these are the rules it applies.
- **Numbers** are rounded to 2 decimal places, and `5` matches `5.0` — so int vs float is

- **Text** is compared exactly: case-sensitive and whitespace-sensitive. `"Closed"` does
not match `"closed"`, and a trailing space matters. When the expected answer is text
copied from elsewhere in the sheet, carry it across verbatim rather than re-typing or
normalizing it — including any trailing space.
- **Type must match** otherwise: the text `"D"` never matches the number `4`. When the
answer is a column heading, a name, or a label, store the `str`; when it is a count or a

lookup, a rolling window, a FIFO allocation or a first-non-zero scan is easier and more
reliable as a loop over cells than as a formula — and unlike a formula it produces the
value the grader reads. Dynamic-array functions (`UNIQUE`, `FILTER`, `TEXTSPLIT`,
`TEXTJOIN`, `SEQUENCE`) and array formulas are the worst case: openpyxl can store no
value for them at all.

row has a start date and an end date that is **blank while the row is still open**, and a

inside the period and every count comes out too **HIGH**. The instruction may define the
measure in those period words even where the graded column's header names a single instant;
for a point-in-time count the header's instant wins.
